summary:
Space Mission Design Game puts students in the seat of a Mission Design Lead. Players pick a science question
about Earth (land cover, coasts or clouds), turn it into six checkable requirements, and design TerraWatch-1, a
fictional low-Earth-orbit satellite mission, across the four segments NASA describes: launch, space, ground and
user. Every choice of launcher, orbit, spacecraft bus, instrument, solar power, radio and ground station updates
live meters for mass, power, energy, battery, data and budget. A deterministic simulation then flies the mission
month by month, shows what the users actually received, explains what held the mission back, and invites a
redesign. In our demo, a weak first design scores 21 out of 100; following the debrief advice, the redesign
scores 100. The game addresses the challenge by making the whole mission system playable, not only the
rocket and spacecraft. It matters because systems thinking and engineering trade-offs are hard to learn from a
textbook and easy to learn by doing.
details:
Space Mission Design Game is a browser game in which the player designs, checks, flies and redesigns a fictional Earth-observation satellite mission called TerraWatch-1. The player chooses one of three science objectives (land cover, coastal change or cloud patterns), each with real users who need the data, and builds the mission across NASA's four segments: launch, space, ground and user.

Every selection is checked live against engineering constraints: mass against launch capacity, peak power against the bus limit, daily solar energy against demand, battery against eclipse, data generated against downlink capacity, and cost against a budget in fictional Mission Units. Twelve hard rules block launch with a plain explanation and a fix; eleven warnings flag weak spots. A deterministic month-by-month simulation then tracks data delivered, backlog, lost data, solar-array ageing and mission events. The results show a science score built from four factors (instrument fit, orbit fit, data delivered and lifetime), the six requirements met or not met, and a "What the users received" panel. The debrief gives up to three prioritised suggestions and a comparison of every run, so the player can redesign and try again. The same inputs always give the same result.

Students see the whole mission system, not just the rocket, and experience how a science goal drives engineering trade-offs. Failure is safe and explained. It runs in any browser on a laptop or phone, needs no installation or account, includes a plain-language glossary, and fits a single lesson. Up to four players can share one device in team roles.

NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions" gives the four mission segments that structure every screen. The Concept Maturity Level framework (via NASA Ames and Goddard) shapes the player's progression from idea to point design, and the Goddard Mission Design Lab's practice of estimating mass, power and data rate shapes the dashboard. "Build It Yourself: Satellite!" inspired the objective-first flow. Thirteen NASA fact cards, each linked to its source, appear in the game. No NASA dataset is loaded; every number is labelled as NASA fact, simplified educational model or fictional game value.

A classroom-ready activity that builds systems thinking and interest in space careers, extended later with more missions (Moon, Mars, constellations) and a teacher view.

HTML, CSS, Tailwind CSS, vanilla JavaScript, vanilla PHP and MySQL/MariaDB, developed on Windows 11 with XAMPP. The server-side engine is covered by 64 automated acceptance tests (including six reference designs), a browser/server agreement check on 1,506 designs, and security tests. Code is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence: https://github.com/hakeemboon/space-mission-design-game

The team chose the concept, the mission and the technology. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with research of the NASA resources, planning documents and test expected values; Claude Code wrote application code and seed data, reviewed by the team, and every generated file carries an "AI-assisted" comment; ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with planning review; Higgsfield generated four decorative background images, each with a visible "SIgenerated" watermark. No generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

This is a simplified educational model, not professional engineering software and not a substitute for NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool. Component values and Mission Units are fictional. Not endorsed or certified by NASA.
